crop_profile.summary: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is an annual fruit crop thriving in warm, humid climates with 18-30°C temperatures, 60-80% humidity, and 500-1000 mm annual rainfall. It prefers loam soils, pH 5.5-7.0, good drainage, and high nitrogen. Drip irrigation, balanced NPK (10-10-10) and organic amendments boost yields of 60-90 t/ha. Major producers include China, India, USA, Turkey, and Egypt. Key challenges are late blight, early blight, Fusarium wilt, and pests like fruit worm, whitefly, and aphids. Proper irrigation, fertilization, timely harvest, and refrigerated storage ensure high-quality marketable fruit.

recommendation.recommendation: Apply organic manure (compost or well‑rotted farmyard manure) to increase soil organic carbon, improve structure, and reduce disease risk.
recommendation.justification: The field shows low organic carbon, high bulk density, and a clay‑loam texture that limit drainage and root growth. Humidity is above the optimal range, raising the risk of foliar diseases. Adding organic manure will raise organic matter, improve soil porosity, enhance moisture retention, and provide a healthier canopy that mitigates disease pressure, aligning with the identified opportunities and mitigating the listed risks.
actions: Source high‑quality compost or well‑rotted farmyard manure (minimum C/N ratio ~12:1).
Apply 5–10 t ha⁻¹ (≈0.5–1 kg m⁻²) evenly across the tomato plot, preferably in the early vegetative stage.
Incorporate the manure into the top 15 cm of soil using a light rotavator or hand tools to avoid further compaction.
Immediately after incorporation, lay a 5–10 cm thick mulch layer (straw, shredded leaves, or black plastic) to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.
Adjust drip irrigation to maintain 20–30 mm week⁻¹, monitoring soil moisture sensors to avoid over‑watering under high humidity.
Conduct a scouting walk within 3 days of application to check for any signs of foliar disease and remove affected foliage promptly.

recommendation.recommendation: Apply organic manure (compost or well‑rotted farmyard manure) to increase soil organic carbon, improve structure, and reduce disease risk.
recommendation.justification: The field shows low organic carbon, high bulk density, and a clay‑loam texture that limit drainage and root growth. Humidity is above the optimal range, raising the risk of foliar diseases. Adding organic manure will raise organic matter, improve soil porosity, enhance moisture retention, and provide a healthier canopy that mitigates disease pressure, aligning with the identified opportunities and mitigating the listed risks.
actions: Source high‑quality compost or well‑rotted farmyard manure (minimum C/N ratio ~12:1).
Apply 5–10 t ha⁻¹ (≈0.5–1 kg m⁻²) evenly across the tomato plot, preferably in the early vegetative stage.
Incorporate the manure into the top 15 cm of soil using a light rotavator or hand tools to avoid further compaction.
Immediately after incorporation, lay a 5–10 cm thick mulch layer (straw, shredded leaves, or black plastic) to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.
Adjust drip irrigation to maintain 20–30 mm week⁻¹, monitoring soil moisture sensors to avoid over‑watering under high humidity.
Conduct a scouting walk within 3 days of application to check for any signs of foliar disease and remove affected foliage promptly.
recommendation.expected_outcome: Improved soil organic carbon and structure will enhance root development, increase water‑use efficiency, and lower the incidence of humidity‑related diseases, leading to higher tomato yields and better market profitability.
monitoring_plan: Soil test for organic carbon 4 weeks after application (target increase of ≥0.5 %).
Weekly NDVI assessment from satellite or drone imagery; aim for NDVI ≥0.65 within 2 weeks.
Bi‑weekly visual scouting for late/early blight symptoms; record any incidence.
Track irrigation volumes and soil moisture sensor readings to keep within the recommended 20–30 mm week⁻¹.
Record plant height and leaf chlorophyll content (SPAD) every 10 days to gauge vegetative vigor.
